primary_authorities.title: California Civil Code § 1946.2 — Just Cause for Residential Tenancy Termination
supports: Tenant Protection Act coverage depends on statutory occupancy thresholds and exemptions; the statute separately defines at-fault and no-fault just cause, owner/family move-in conditions, withdrawal/government-order/substantial-remodel grounds, relocation rules, exemption conditions, and interaction with qualifying more-protective local ordinances.

primary_authorities.title: California Civil Code § 1946.1 — Periodic Tenancy Termination Notice
supports: Statewide 60-day owner termination baseline and specified 30-day owner termination situations for periodic residential tenancies.

primary_authorities.title: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1161 — Unlawful Detainer Grounds and Three-Day Notices
supports: CCP §1161(2) and (3) expressly exclude Saturdays, Sundays, and judicial holidays for curable pay-rent and covenant notices; §1161(4) separately authorizes three days notice to quit for specified assignment/subletting, waste, nuisance, and unlawful-use grounds without repeating those curable-notice exclusions.

primary_authorities.title: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1167 — Unlawful Detainer Summons Response Time
supports: Unlawful-detainer response is due within 10 days excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and judicial holidays after service, with specified extra time for Safe at Home service.

primary_authorities.title: California Civil Code § 789.3 — Utility Interruption and Self-Help Lockout Prohibitions
supports: Residential landlords may not willfully interrupt utilities, change locks, remove doors/windows, or remove tenant property with intent to terminate occupancy outside lawful process; statute provides civil remedies.

primary_authorities.title: California Government Code § 12927 — Housing Discrimination Definitions
supports: California housing discrimination includes cancellation or termination of a rental agreement and refusal to provide reasonable accommodation or modification when statutory conditions are met.

primary_authorities.title: California Government Code § 12955 — Housing Discrimination Prohibited
supports: California prohibits specified housing discrimination, discriminatory eviction/retaliation, and source-of-income discrimination including covered housing vouchers and HUD-VASH.

primary_authorities.title: California Courts — Starting an Eviction: Notice Deadline Counting
supports: California Courts explains that curable three-day notice periods exclude weekends/court holidays while 30- and 60-day termination notices count calendar days.

primary_authorities.title: California Courts — Fill Out an Answer in an Eviction Case
supports: Current unlawful-detainer response instructions, including UD-105, personal-service 10 court-day response, substituted/posting service mixed computation, Safe at Home timing, and local-form warning.

primary_authorities.title: California Courts — Default Judgment in Eviction
supports: After the response deadline passes without a response, the landlord may seek default; an answer may still be filed before default is requested, and current default forms/process are identified.

primary_authorities.title: California Courts — What Happens if You Lose an Eviction Case
supports: Post-judgment writ/sheriff process, five-day Notice to Vacate, stay-of-execution option, set-aside possibility, and warning that appeal alone does not stop sheriff eviction.

primary_authorities.title: Judicial Council of California — Eviction Forms
supports: Current statewide eviction forms include SUM-130, UD-100, UD-105, UD-110, UD-116, and UD-150, with current effective dates.

primary_authorities.title: Judicial Branch of California — Find Your Court / Local Rules and Forms
supports: California has county Superior Courts with local rules/forms; users must identify the actual court and check its current local requirements.

primary_authorities.title: California Civil Rights Department — Housing
supports: State fair-housing complaint forum, one-year administrative filing guidance, reasonable accommodation examples, and distinction between discrimination enforcement and ordinary landlord-tenant disputes.

local_variation.statewide_rule: California statutes and statewide Judicial Council rules/forms provide the baseline, but local just-cause/rent-control ordinances and Superior Court local rules/forms may add protections or procedure. Section 1946.2 expressly preserves qualifying more-protective local just-cause ordinances.

notice_pay_rent_or_quit.label: NOTICE TO PAY RENT OR QUIT
notice_pay_rent_or_quit.description: For nonpayment of rent under CCP §1161(2), the statutory three-day cure period excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays. The notice must satisfy statutory content and service requirements; do not generalize this route to every eviction notice.
notice_pay_rent_or_quit.court_or_forum: Pre-suit; Superior Court if unlawful detainer is later filed

optional_actions.text: Save the notice, proof of service, lease, rent ledger, payment records, and communications.

exceptions: Notice validity, rent amount/content, and service method are fact-specific.
immediate_clock.display: For a qualifying pay-rent-or-quit notice under CCP §1161(2), the three-day period excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and judicial holidays.

possession_consequences: If the notice expires without cure and the landlord otherwise complies with law, the landlord may file an unlawful-detainer case; the notice itself is not a court judgment.

local_variation.statewide_rule: California statewide baseline; local substantive protections and court procedure may add requirements.

notice_perform_covenant_or_quit.label: NOTICE TO PERFORM COVENANT OR QUIT
notice_perform_covenant_or_quit.description: For a curable non-rent lease violation under CCP §1161(3), the three-day period excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and judicial holidays; the Tenant Protection Act can require an opportunity to cure before a later no-cure termination where its just-cause rules apply.
notice_perform_covenant_or_quit.court_or_forum: Pre-suit; Superior Court if unlawful detainer is later filed

optional_actions.text: Identify the exact lease term alleged to be violated and preserve proof of any cure or accommodation request.

exceptions: Whether a breach is curable and whether additional just-cause protections apply depends on the tenancy and facts.
immediate_clock.display: For a qualifying perform-covenant-or-quit notice under CCP §1161(3), the three-day cure period excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and judicial holidays.

local_variation.statewide_rule: California statewide baseline; local substantive protections and court procedure may add requirements.

notice_quit_breach_nuisance.label: NOTICE TO QUIT — ALLEGED NONCURABLE BREACH / NUISANCE
notice_quit_breach_nuisance.description: CCP §1161(4) authorizes three days notice to quit for specified assignment/subletting, waste, nuisance, and unlawful-use grounds. Unlike §1161(2) and (3), paragraph (4) does not itself repeat the Saturday/Sunday/judicial-holiday exclusion used for the curable notice categories. Because service and generally applicable computation rules still require separate verification, no actionable clock is published here.
notice_quit_breach_nuisance.court_or_forum: Pre-suit; Superior Court if unlawful detainer is later filed

optional_actions.text: Save the notice and all evidence concerning the alleged conduct; get legal help quickly because whether the ground is legally noncurable can be contested.

exceptions: Whether alleged conduct legally qualifies under §1161(4), whether Tenant Protection Act or local just-cause requirements add protections, and the exact computation after service are fact- and authority-specific.

local_variation.statewide_rule: California statewide baseline; local substantive protections and court procedure may add requirements.

termination_30_day.label: 30-DAY TERMINATION NOTICE
termination_30_day.description: Civil Code §1946.1 provides specified situations in which an owner may use at least 30 days' notice for periodic tenancy termination, including generally where the tenant/resident has occupied the dwelling for less than one year and a separate sale-related rule. This does not override applicable just-cause protections.

optional_actions.text: Check length of occupancy, lease type, Tenant Protection Act coverage, and any local just-cause ordinance before assuming a 30-day notice is valid.

exceptions: Civil Code §1946.1 contains applicability conditions and exceptions; just-cause law may independently restrict termination.
immediate_clock.display: A qualifying 30-day termination notice under Civil Code §1946.1 is counted in calendar days; applicability depends on the tenancy and statutory conditions.

local_variation.statewide_rule: California statewide baseline; local substantive protections and court procedure may add requirements.

termination_60_day.label: 60-DAY TERMINATION NOTICE
termination_60_day.description: Civil Code §1946.1 states a general owner baseline of at least 60 days before the proposed termination of a qualifying periodic residential tenancy, subject to statutory 30-day situations and separate just-cause/local-law restrictions.

optional_actions.text: Check Tenant Protection Act coverage and local just-cause/rent-control law before treating a 60-day notice as sufficient by itself.

exceptions: Section 1946.1 has 30-day exceptions and does not eliminate just-cause or more-protective local requirements.
immediate_clock.display: For a qualifying periodic tenancy, Civil Code §1946.1 generally requires at least 60 days' owner notice; California Courts counts 30- and 60-day termination notices in calendar days.

local_variation.statewide_rule: California statewide baseline; local substantive protections and court procedure may add requirements.

just_cause_termination.label: JUST-CAUSE / NO-FAULT JUST-CAUSE TERMINATION
just_cause_termination.description: Civil Code §1946.2 requires just cause only for covered tenancies after the statute’s occupancy thresholds. It separately defines at-fault and no-fault grounds, contains category-specific exemptions and notice conditions, and preserves qualifying more-protective local ordinances. A verified statute is not a universal entitlement: applicability must be checked for the actual tenancy.

optional_actions.text: Check occupancy duration, property type/ownership, exemption notice language, the stated cause, and local ordinance coverage before deciding whether §1946.2 applies.

other_clocks.label: No-fault relocation payment timing
exceptions: Owner may instead elect a written final-month rent waiver as allowed by the statute; local law may provide different or greater relocation rights.
other_clocks.display: For a covered no-fault just-cause termination where the owner elects direct relocation payment, Civil Code §1946.2 requires payment within 15 calendar days of service of the notice.

exceptions: Not all California residential tenancies are covered by §1946.2; occupancy thresholds, property/ownership categories, exemption notice conditions, mobilehome rules, and qualifying local ordinances matter.
Do not summarize the statute as one year equals just cause or all single-family homes are exempt.

local_variation.statewide_rule: California statewide baseline; qualifying more-protective local just-cause ordinances may control.

summons_unlawful_detainer.label: SUMMONS + UNLAWFUL DETAINER COMPLAINT
summons_unlawful_detainer.description: A residential unlawful-detainer case is filed in California Superior Court. The response deadline depends on service method. Personal/direct service uses a 10 court-day clock; substituted service/posting can use a mixed service-completion calculation. Current statewide forms include SUM-130, UD-100, and UD-105.
summons_unlawful_detainer.court_or_forum: California Superior Court in the county/courthouse handling the rental-property eviction

required_actions.text: To contest the eviction through an Answer, file a timely response in the Superior Court case; current California Courts guidance identifies form UD-105 as the main Answer form.

optional_actions.text: Record exactly how and when the Summons and Complaint were served, because service method changes the response computation.
Check the actual Superior Court for local forms or filing requirements.

summons_unlawful_detainer.required_filing: Answer—Unlawful Detainer (UD-105) is the main statewide answer form; other responsive pleadings can exist and may require legal help.

exceptions: Substituted service, posting plus mailing, and Safe at Home service use different completion/timing rules; do not apply this 10-day trigger blindly.
immediate_clock.display: After personal/direct service of an unlawful-detainer Summons and Complaint, CCP §1167 requires a response within 10 days excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays.

other_clocks.label: Substituted service or posting plus mailing
exceptions: Use the actual proof of service and current court instructions; this is not the same computation as personal service.
other_clocks.display: California Courts explains that substituted service or posting plus mailing generally produces a 20-day mixed computation: 10 calendar days to complete service, then 10 court days to respond.

possession_consequences: If no timely response is filed and default is entered, the court can proceed without hearing the tenant's defenses unless relief from default is later obtained.

local_variation.statewide_rule: Statewide forms and response law apply, but Superior Courts may require local forms or procedures.

default_requested_or_entered.label: REQUEST FOR ENTRY OF DEFAULT / DEFAULT ENTERED
default_requested_or_entered.description: After the response deadline passes without a response, the landlord may request default. California Courts states that a tenant may still file an Answer before the landlord asks for default; once default is entered, ordinary filing of an Answer is no longer the route and immediate legal help is appropriate.

optional_actions.text: If default has already been entered, seek immediate court self-help or legal counsel about possible relief; this repository does not prescribe an individualized motion strategy.

possession_consequences: Default can lead to a possession judgment and sheriff enforcement without a contested trial.

local_variation.statewide_rule: Statewide baseline; local filing procedure may add requirements.

judgment_post_trial.label: JUDGMENT — APPEAL / STAY / WRIT
judgment_post_trial.description: After an eviction judgment for the landlord, appeal, stay, set-aside relief, and sheriff enforcement are separate concepts. California Courts expressly warns that filing an appeal does not itself stop the sheriff from evicting the tenant.
judgment_post_trial.court_or_forum: California Superior Court / appellate court as applicable

optional_actions.text: Get the signed judgment and any issued writ/Notice to Vacate, and identify whether a stay has actually been granted rather than assuming an appeal stops enforcement.

remedies: Possible post-judgment routes can include appeal, stay of execution, or set-aside relief depending on facts and procedural posture.
possession_consequences: An appeal alone does not stop sheriff eviction according to current California Courts guidance.

local_variation.statewide_rule: Statewide baseline; local filing procedure may add requirements.

sheriff_notice_to_vacate.label: SHERIFF NOTICE TO VACATE / WRIT OF POSSESSION
sheriff_notice_to_vacate.description: After a possession judgment and issuance of the writ, the landlord delivers the writ to the sheriff. California Courts states that the sheriff gives a Notice to Vacate allowing five days to move; if the deadline passes without a stay or other effective relief, the sheriff may return and lock the occupants out.
sheriff_notice_to_vacate.court_or_forum: California Superior Court / county sheriff executing writ

optional_actions.text: Use the posted sheriff Notice to Vacate for the exact enforcement deadline and seek immediate legal/self-help assistance if a stay or other relief may be available.

exceptions: County operational steps can vary; the posted notice controls the actual move-out date/time. A court-ordered stay or other effective relief can change enforcement.
immediate_clock.display: California Courts states that the sheriff's Notice to Vacate gives the tenant five days to move; use the posted notice for the exact lockout deadline.

remedies: A tenant may ask the court for a stay of execution; an appeal alone does not automatically stop the sheriff.
possession_consequences: After the notice period, absent effective relief, the sheriff may physically remove occupants and restore possession to the landlord.

local_variation.statewide_rule: The statewide writ/Notice to Vacate framework applies, while sheriff operational practice can vary by county.

self_help_lockout.label: LANDLORD CHANGED LOCKS / REMOVED ME WITHOUT COURT PROCESS
self_help_lockout.description: Civil Code §789.3 prohibits specified willful self-help measures intended to terminate residential occupancy, including changing locks, removing doors/windows, and removing tenant property outside lawful procedures. Lawful sheriff eviction is distinct.
self_help_lockout.court_or_forum: Civil court / emergency legal-help pathway depending remedy

optional_actions.text: Document the lock change/removal, preserve communications and photographs, and seek immediate legal help if access to the home is being denied.

remedies: Section 789.3 provides a civil damages remedy and permits appropriate injunctive relief; other remedies may also exist.
exceptions: The statute does not prohibit lawful eviction carried out by appropriate legal authorities.

local_variation.statewide_rule: Statewide statutory protection; local emergency resources may vary.

utility_shutoff.label: LANDLORD-CAUSED UTILITY SHUTOFF
utility_shutoff.description: Civil Code §789.3 prohibits a landlord from willfully causing interruption or termination of specified utilities with intent to terminate residential occupancy. This route concerns landlord self-help, not ordinary utility-company termination for account/service reasons.
utility_shutoff.court_or_forum: Civil court / emergency legal-help pathway depending remedy

optional_actions.text: Document which service stopped, when, who caused it, notices/account status, and landlord communications; seek emergency legal help where health or housing is at immediate risk.

remedies: Section 789.3 provides civil damages and permits appropriate injunctive relief for covered landlord conduct.
exceptions: Do not treat every utility outage or utility-provider termination as a landlord violation.

local_variation.statewide_rule: Statewide statutory protection; local emergency resources may vary.

state_fair_housing.label: CALIFORNIA FAIR-HOUSING / REASONABLE ACCOMMODATION
state_fair_housing.description: California FEHA housing protections are a distinct state-law layer. Government Code §§12927 and 12955 address discrimination, cancellation/termination of rental agreements, retaliation, reasonable accommodation/modification, protected characteristics, and source-of-income protections including covered vouchers.
state_fair_housing.court_or_forum: California Civil Rights Department and/or court depending claim

optional_actions.text: Preserve the accommodation request, disability-related nexus information actually needed, provider response, eviction papers, and proof of timing; do not assume accommodation automatically stops an eviction.

other_clocks.label: CRD housing-discrimination administrative complaint
exceptions: Judicial filing periods and tolling rules can differ; this clock is only the general CRD administrative-complaint guidance.
other_clocks.display: California CRD states that, in general, a housing-discrimination complaint must be filed within one year of the alleged discriminatory act.

exceptions: State FEHA and the federal Fair Housing Act are separate provenance layers; neither makes every accommodation request an automatic eviction stay.

local_variation.statewide_rule: State FEHA is a statewide layer; local civil-rights or tenant ordinances can add separate protections.

federal_fair_housing_overlay.label: FEDERAL FAIR HOUSING ACT OVERLAY
federal_fair_housing_overlay.description: Federal Fair Housing Act reasonable-accommodation protection is reused from the federal housing overlay rather than restated as California law. It must remain separate from California FEHA.
exceptions: This route is an overlay reference, not California statutory authority and not an automatic defense to every eviction.

local_variation.statewide_rule: Federal overlay remains separate from California law.

subsidized_housing_termination.label: SUBSIDIZED-HOUSING TERMINATION / VOUCHER ACTION
subsidized_housing_termination.description: Public housing, Housing Choice Voucher, project-based assistance, and HUD-VASH can create program-specific notice/review layers separate from the landlord's California unlawful-detainer case. This first California core does not yet publish program-specific deadlines.

optional_actions.text: Identify whether the paper came from the landlord, PHA, voucher administrator, or project-based housing provider; preserve both program notices and court papers.

exceptions: Do not collapse loss of assistance and state-court eviction into one decision or one appeal.

local_variation.statewide_rule: Federal program procedure is separate from California eviction law; local PHA administration varies.

california_courts_self_help.name: California Courts Self-Help — Eviction
california_courts_self_help.coverage: Statewide court self-help information and court locator

california_civil_rights.name: California Civil Rights Department — Housing
california_civil_rights.eligibility_notes: Handles discrimination matters; does not represent tenants in ordinary unlawful-detainer cases.
